content: Daptomycin is indicated for the treatment of right-sided infective endocarditis caused by methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant isolates. The recommended dosage is 6 mg/kg administered intravenously every 24 hours for a duration of 2 to 6 weeks. However, safety data for use beyond 28 days is limited; in a phase 3 trial, only 14 adults were treated for more than 28 days. It is also indicated for the treatment of complicated skin and skin structure infections (cSSSI) caused by susceptible isolates, with a recommended dosage of 4 mg/kg intravenously every 24 hours for 7 to 14 days. To minimize the development of drug-resistant bacteria and maintain the effectiveness of antibacterial drugs, daptomycin should only be used to treat or prevent infections that are proven or strongly suspected to be caused by bacteria. The safety and efficacy of daptomycin in children under 1 year of age or in those with renal impairment have not been established. For children with renal impairment, no specific dosage regimen has been determined. Daptomycin interacts with several drugs and vaccines. Co-administration with the cholera vaccine should be avoided, as systemic antibiotics may inactivate the vaccine strain. Cholera vaccination should not be administered to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. Similarly, daptomycin may reduce the efficacy of oral microbiota products containing bacterial spores due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Antibiotic regimens should be completed 2 to 4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. When daptomycin is co-administered with HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins such as atorvastatin, fluvastatin, lovastatin, pitavastatin, pravastatin, rosuvastatin, and simvastatin), there is an increased risk of elevated creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels and myopathy. Temporary suspension of the statin during daptomycin therapy should be considered, and therapy should be closely monitored. Additionally, daptomycin may decrease the effects of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering colonic bacterial flora needed for drug activation. Caution and monitoring are advised in such cases. Daptomycin may also interact with tobramycin, leading to decreased tobramycin levels and increased daptomycin levels when co-administered. The mechanism of this interaction is unspecified, but close monitoring is recommended. Serious immune system reactions have been reported with daptomycin, including anaphylaxis, angioedema, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), pruritus, hives, shortness of breath, difficulty swallowing, truncal erythema, and pulmonary eosinophilia. Systemic steroids may be required for treatment. Other adverse effects include Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea, increased myoglobin levels, rhabdomyolysis, eosinophilic pneumonia, organizing pneumonia, peripheral neuropathy, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, vesiculobullous rash, nausea, vomiting, visual disturbances, anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, acute kidney injury, renal insufficiency, renal failure, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, epidermal necrolysis, and toxic epidermal necrolysis. If hypersensitivity reactions occur, the drug should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate therapy should be initiated. Eosinophilic pneumonia, a potentially fatal condition characterized by fever, cough, shortness of breath, and difficulty breathing, has been associated with daptomycin. Prompt medical evaluation and discontinuation of the drug are necessary if symptoms develop. Systemic steroids are recommended for treatment. Prolonged use of daptomycin may result in fungal or bacterial superinfections. Persistent or relapsing infections should prompt susceptibility testing and evaluation for sequestered infection foci. Daptomycin is excreted in breast milk at approximately 1% of the maternal dose. There is no information on its effects on breastfed infants or milk production. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for therapy and potential adverse effects on the infant. Daptomycin is generally considered safe during pregnancy, with no evidence of fetal risk in controlled studies. The drug is available in three formulations with specific storage and reconstitution requirements. Cubicin should be refrigerated at 2–8°C (36–46°F). Cubicin RF and Dapzura RT can be stored at controlled room temperature (20–25°C or 68–77°F) with excursions permitted to 15–30°C (59–86°F). Daptomycin 350 mg vials should be refrigerated at 2–8°C (36–46°F) but can be stored at room temperature for up to 12 hours or refrigerated for up to 48 hours after reconstitution. Proper storage and handling instructions should be followed as per the labeling. This information is provided for general educational purposes. Formulary details may vary, and it is recommended to contact the applicable plan provider for the most current information.
